topics.kicker: Rocks formed from cooled magma or lava · One of the three main rock types
topics.dates: Form whenever magma or lava cools and hardens
topics.briefing: Igneous rocks are “fire-formed” rocks: their name comes from the Latin word for fire, because they harden from molten magma or lava. Magma that cools slowly underground grows big crystals, making coarse rocks like granite, while lava that cools fast at the surface keeps its crystals tiny, as in basalt, or freezes into glassy obsidian. Along with sedimentary and metamorphic rocks, they are one of the three main kinds of rock.
topics.answerHtml: Igneous rocks (accept intrusive or extrusive igneous rocks or magmatic rocks; prompt on volcanic rocks, plutonic rocks, intrusive rocks, or extrusive rocks; do not accept “sedimentary rocks,” “metamorphic rocks,” “magma,” or “lava”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Norman Bowen’s reaction series lists the order in which minerals crystallize from the molten material that forms these rocks, starting with olivine and ending with quartz. Bowen worked out that order by melting and cooling rock samples in a laboratory.
tossups.r: These rocks are called extrusive if they cool quickly at the surface. For 10 points, name this class of rocks that form when magma or lava cools and hardens.

tossups.p: Andesite, an example of these rocks whose name comes from South America’s Andes Mountains, erupts from many volcanoes above subduction zones. Diorite, a speckled “salt-and-pepper” example of these rocks, has the same minerals as andesite but cooled slowly underground.
tossups.r: Light felsic examples like granite are rich in silica, unlike dark mafic ones like basalt. For 10 points, name these rocks that harden from magma or lava.

tossups.p: Most of the giant moai [“MOH-eye”] statues of Easter Island were carved from tuff, an example of these rocks made of volcanic ash that hardened into stone. Wind and water carved the cone-shaped “fairy chimneys” of Turkey’s Cappadocia region out of thick layers of tuff, too.
tossups.r: Obsidian is a glassy example of these rocks that cooled too fast to grow crystals. For 10 points, name these rocks that form when molten magma or lava solidifies.

tossups.p: Peridotite, a green example of these rocks named for the gem peridot, is made mostly of olivine and makes up most of Earth’s upper mantle. Its makeup is called ultramafic, because it holds even less silica than mafic rocks do.
tossups.r: Dark, iron-rich examples of these rocks, like basalt and gabbro, are called mafic. For 10 points, name this rock type that forms when magma or lava cools.

tossups.p: New Mexico’s Shiprock, a peak sacred to the Navajo people, is the eroded throat of an ancient volcano made of these rocks, with long, wall-like dikes radiating out from it. Those dikes formed when molten rock squeezed into cracks and hardened.
tossups.r: Sheets of these rocks that slip between rock layers are called sills. For 10 points, name these rocks, including granite and basalt, that form from cooled magma or lava.

tossups.p: Wyoming’s Devils Tower, the first U.S. national monument and the alien landing site in the film _Close Encounters of the Third Kind_, is a giant mass of these rocks that cracked into tall columns. It was left standing after softer sedimentary rock around it wore away.
tossups.r: Similar columns of these rocks form Northern Ireland’s Giant’s Causeway. For 10 points, name this rock type that forms when magma or lava cools.

tossups.p: After studying Utah’s Henry Mountains in the 1870s, Grove Karl Gilbert described laccoliths, mushroom-shaped masses of these rocks that bowed the layers above them up into domes. Gilbert showed that those masses had pushed in as molten rock between existing rock layers.
tossups.r: Much larger underground masses of these rocks, called batholiths, form the cores of ranges like the Sierra Nevada. For 10 points, name this class of rocks that form when magma or lava cools.

tossups.p: Chunks of older rock that fell into molten material and got trapped as it hardened into these rocks are called xenoliths [“ZEN-uh-liths”], from Greek words meaning “foreign stones.” Such chunks must be older than the rock that surrounds them.
tossups.r: Magma that cools slowly underground into these rocks grows large crystals, as in granite. For 10 points, name this class of rocks that harden from magma or lava.

tossups.p: These rocks are the best kind for radiometric dating, because the atomic “clocks” in their minerals start ticking when the molten material crystallizes. Dating layers of these rocks found above and below a fossil can bracket that fossil’s age.
tossups.r: They form one of the three main rock types, with sedimentary and metamorphic rocks. For 10 points, name this rock type named from the Latin word for “fire.”

tossups.p: James Hutton’s followers, called Plutonists, argued that rocks of this type formed from molten material deep inside Earth, rather than settling out of an ancient ocean as Abraham Werner’s Neptunists believed. Both Plutonism and some of these rocks are named for the Roman god of the underworld.
tossups.r: Examples of these rocks that cool slowly underground are called intrusive or plutonic. For 10 points, name this class of rocks that form from cooled magma or lava.

tossups.p: The Moon’s bright highlands are made of anorthosite [“an-OR-thuh-site”], an example of these rocks that formed as an ocean of molten rock covering the young Moon cooled and its light crystals floated to the top. The dark lunar maria [“MAR-ee-uh”] are also made of these rocks.
tossups.r: Pumice, an example of these rocks full of gas bubbles, can float on water. For 10 points, name this class of rocks that form when magma or lava cools.

tossups.p: Geologists call the texture of these rocks aphanitic [“af-uh-NIT-ik”] when their crystals are too small to see, phaneritic [“fan-uh-RIT-ik”] when the crystals are visible to the naked eye, and pegmatitic when the crystals are enormous. Those textures depend mostly on how fast the molten material cooled.
tossups.r: Examples with big crystals scattered in a fine background are called porphyritic. For 10 points, name this rock type that forms when magma or lava cools and hardens.

tossups.p: The Siberian Traps, a giant staircase of these rocks built by enormous floods of molten rock, are linked to the end-Permian mass extinction about 252 million years ago. India’s Deccan Traps, another huge pile of these rocks, formed around the time the dinosaurs died out.
tossups.r: Quickly cooled, extrusive examples of these rocks have tiny crystals. For 10 points, name these rocks, such as basalt and granite, that form from cooled magma or lava.

tossups.p: Diamonds reach Earth’s surface inside kimberlite, an example of these rocks that blasted up through narrow, carrot-shaped pipes from deep in the mantle. South Africa’s “Big Hole” at Kimberley was dug largely by hand to mine one of those pipes.
tossups.r: Gas bubbles called vesicles fill some of these rocks, like pumice and scoria. For 10 points, name this class of rocks that form when magma or lava cools.

tossups.p: A porphyritic [“por-fuh-RIT-ik”] example of these rocks has large crystals called phenocrysts [“FEE-nuh-krists”] scattered through a fine-grained background, a sign that its molten material began cooling slowly underground, growing big crystals, and then finished cooling quickly at the surface.
tossups.r: Obsidian is a glassy example of these rocks. For 10 points, name this rock type, one of the three main types along with sedimentary and metamorphic rocks.

clues.t: Rocks that form when molten magma or lava cools and hardens
Their name comes from the Latin word ignis, meaning “fire”
One of the three main rock types in the rock cycle, along with sedimentary and metamorphic rocks
Examples include granite, basalt, obsidian, and pumice
Intrusive (plutonic) kinds cool slowly underground; extrusive (volcanic) kinds cool quickly at the surface
Slow cooling grows big crystals, as in coarse-grained granite; fast cooling leaves tiny crystals, as in fine-grained basalt
Obsidian is natural volcanic glass that cooled too fast to grow any crystals
Gas bubbles leave holes called vesicles, as in scoria; bubbly pumice can even float on water
Sorted by silica: light felsic kinds like granite are silica-rich, while dark mafic kinds like basalt and gabbro are rich in magnesium and iron
“Plutonic” kinds are named for Pluto, the Roman god of the underworld
Molten rock squeezed into cracks hardens into dikes, which cut across rock layers, and sills, which slip between them
Porphyritic kinds have large crystals (phenocrysts) in a fine background, a sign they cooled in two stages
Thick masses that cool and shrink can crack into tall columns, as at Northern Ireland’s Giant’s Causeway
Huge underground masses called batholiths form the cores of mountain ranges like the Sierra Nevada
Norman Bowen’s reaction series gives the order in which minerals crystallize from cooling magma, from olivine first to quartz last
Andesite, named for the Andes, erupts above subduction zones; speckled “salt-and-pepper” diorite has the same minerals but cooled slowly underground
Tuff, volcanic ash hardened into stone, was carved into most of Easter Island’s moai and eroded into Cappadocia’s “fairy chimneys”
Peridotite, a green, olivine-rich kind named for the gem peridot, makes up most of the upper mantle
Diamonds ride up from the mantle inside kimberlite, which fills carrot-shaped pipes like the one dug out at Kimberley’s “Big Hole”
New Mexico’s Shiprock, sacred to the Navajo, is an ancient volcano’s eroded throat with dikes radiating from it
Wyoming’s Devils Tower, the first U.S. national monument, is a columned mass left standing after softer rock eroded
G. K. Gilbert described mushroom-shaped laccoliths, which dome up the layers above them, in Utah’s Henry Mountains
Trapped chunks of older rock are called xenoliths, Greek for “foreign stones,” and must be older than the rock around them
Best for radiometric dating, since their minerals’ atomic “clocks” start when they crystallize; layers of them can bracket a fossil’s age
James Hutton’s Plutonists said they formed from molten rock, against Abraham Werner’s Neptunists, who said they settled out of an ocean
The Moon’s bright highlands are anorthosite, formed as an ancient ocean of molten rock cooled; its dark maria are this kind of rock too
Textures with crystals too small to see are aphanitic, visible ones phaneritic, and giant ones pegmatitic
The Siberian Traps, a vast pile of flood lava, are linked to the end-Permian extinction; India’s Deccan Traps formed around when the dinosaurs died out

trap.title: The class, not one rock
trap.body: Igneous-rock tossups are packed with examples like granite, basalt, obsidian, and pumice, and with the words magma and lava, which tempts players to buzz with one of them. The question wants the whole class of rocks. The other two classes trip players up too: sedimentary rocks form from pressed-together sediment, and metamorphic rocks are changed by heat and pressure without melting.
trap.fix: Listen for “this class of rocks” or “these rocks.” Molten material, crystal size, plutonic, or volcanic means igneous; layers, fossils, and cementing mean sedimentary; squeezing, banding, and heat without melting mean metamorphic. Saying “volcanic rocks” or “plutonic rocks” earns only a prompt.
trap.line: Real answer line: Igneous rocks (prompt on volcanic rocks or plutonic rocks; do not accept “sedimentary rocks,” “metamorphic rocks,” “magma,” or “lava”)

topics.name: Rivers
topics.kicker: Natural channels of flowing fresh water · Carve valleys and build deltas
topics.dates: Carry rain and snowmelt downhill to the sea
topics.briefing: Rivers are Earth’s great movers: they carry rain and melted snow downhill toward the sea, carving valleys and canyons as they go. The Colorado River cut the Grand Canyon, the Mississippi drains parts of more than 30 states, and the Amazon pours more water into the ocean than any other river. Where a river finally slows down at its mouth, it drops its mud and sand to build a delta.
topics.answerHtml: Rivers (accept streams; prompt on creeks or running water; do not accept “lakes,” “deltas,” “tributaries,” or the name of one specific river)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: One of these in western Turkey, known to the ancient Greeks as the Maeander [“mee-AN-der”], wound back and forth so much that its name became the English word for such loops. In Australia, a loop that has been cut off from one of these is called a billabong.
tossups.r: Fast water on the outside of each bend carves a steep cut bank. For 10 points, name these flowing bodies of fresh water, such as the Nile and the Amazon.

tossups.p: The scientific study of these features is called potamology, from a Greek word that also forms part of the name of the hippopotamus. Processes caused by these features are called fluvial, from the Latin word for them.
tossups.r: Smaller ones called tributaries join to form bigger ones. For 10 points, name these bodies of flowing fresh water that carve valleys as they run downhill to the sea.

tossups.p: Mesopotamia’s name comes from Greek words meaning the land “between” two of these features. Farmers there dug canals to spread the water of those two, which flood in spring with melted snow from the mountains of what is now Turkey.
tossups.r: Those two, the Tigris and the Euphrates, spread fertile mud across their floodplains. For 10 points, name these flowing bodies of fresh water, like the Nile.

tossups.p: The Hjulström [“YOOL-strum”] curve shows how fast the water in one of these must flow to pick up, carry, or drop grains of each size. Oddly, it takes faster water to lift tiny clay particles than sand, because clay grains stick together.
tossups.r: These features carry sediment as dissolved load, suspended load, and bed load. For 10 points, name these flowing bodies of fresh water that carve valleys and canyons.

tossups.p: Arthur Strahler’s ordering system, which built on earlier work by Robert Horton, ranks the smallest of these, with nothing flowing into them, as “first-order.” When two first-order ones meet, they form a “second-order” one, and so on up the scale.
tossups.r: The land that drains into one of these is its drainage basin, or watershed. For 10 points, name these bodies of flowing water, such as the Mississippi.

tossups.p: Treaties often set borders along the thalweg [“TAHL-veg”] of one of these, the line that follows its deepest channel, from German words meaning “valley way.” A change of course by one of these near El Paso led to the Chamizal [“chah-mee-ZAHL”] border dispute between the United States and Mexico.
tossups.r: These features drop sand and mud where they meet the sea, building deltas. For 10 points, name these flowing bodies of fresh water, like the Nile and the Amazon.

tossups.p: After leading the first known boat trip through the Grand Canyon in 1869, John Wesley Powell named the idea of base level, the lowest point to which one of these can wear down its bed. For most of these features, base level is sea level.
tossups.r: Young, steep ones carve V-shaped valleys, unlike the U-shaped valleys made by glaciers. For 10 points, name these flowing bodies of water, such as the Colorado.

tossups.p: In a process called capture or “piracy,” one of these wears its way back into the land beyond its source until it steals the water of a neighbor. That headward erosion lets the thief grow longer at its upper end.
tossups.r: Where one of these meets the sea, fresh and salt water mix in a brackish estuary. For 10 points, name these flowing bodies of fresh water.

tossups.p: Tributaries called Yazoo [“YAZ-oo”] types, named for one in the state of Mississippi, run alongside a bigger one of these for miles because natural levees block them from joining it. Those levees build up when floodwater drops its heaviest sediment right beside the banks.
tossups.r: Floods also spread fine mud across flat floodplains. For 10 points, name these flowing bodies of water, such as the Mississippi.

tossups.p: A swagman camps beside a billabong in the song “Waltzing Matilda,” using an Australian word for a loop that has been cut off from one of these. Such cut-off loops form when the narrow neck of land between two bends wears through, often during a flood.
tossups.r: Elsewhere those cut-off loops are called oxbow lakes. For 10 points, name these flowing bodies of fresh water whose winding loops are called meanders.

tossups.p: Arizona’s Horseshoe Bend and Utah’s Goosenecks are deep, looping canyons called incised meanders, carved as the land slowly rose while these features kept cutting downward. Trapped between rock walls, such loops can no longer shift sideways.
tossups.r: The Colorado and the San Juan carved those two canyons. For 10 points, name these flowing bodies of fresh water that carve valleys and canyons.

tossups.p: Ecologists call the strip of land and plants along the banks of one of these its riparian [“rih-PAIR-ee-un”] zone, from a Latin word for “bank.” Sediment these features leave behind is called alluvium, and fans of it spread out where they leave the mountains.
tossups.r: Their discharge, the volume of water flowing past a point each second, is greatest for the Amazon. For 10 points, name these flowing bodies of fresh water.

tossups.p: Niagara Falls is a knickpoint, a sudden step in the slope of one of these, and it has slowly worn its way miles back toward Lake Erie as water undercuts its hard top layer of rock, which then breaks off. Many such waterfalls form where water crosses from hard rock onto softer rock.
tossups.r: These features’ winding loops are called meanders. For 10 points, name these flowing bodies of fresh water, such as the Nile and the Amazon.

tossups.p: A hydrograph plots how much water one of these carries over time, and its lag time is the delay between the heaviest rain and the highest flow. Paving over land shortens that lag, because rain rushes off instead of soaking into the ground.
tossups.r: The volume of water flowing past a point each second is called discharge. For 10 points, name these flowing bodies of water that carry rain and snowmelt to the sea.

tossups.p: Braided examples of these features split into many shallow channels around bars of sand and gravel, especially below melting glaciers. Other examples wind back and forth in loops called meanders, which can be cut off to form oxbow lakes.
tossups.r: Where they slow down at the sea, they drop sediment to build deltas. For 10 points, name these flowing bodies of fresh water, like the Nile, the Amazon, and the Mississippi.

clues.t: Natural channels of flowing fresh water that run downhill from a source, or headwaters, to a mouth, usually at the sea
Famous examples include the Nile, the Amazon, the Mississippi, and the Yangtze
Running water is the leading cause of erosion on land, carving valleys and canyons like the Grand Canyon
Smaller ones that flow into a bigger one are called tributaries
Their winding loops are called meanders; a loop that gets cut off becomes a curved oxbow lake
On a bend, fast water erodes the outer bank into a cut bank, while slow water builds a point bar on the inner bank
Sediment dropped at the mouth builds a delta, named for the triangle-shaped Greek letter; the Mississippi’s is a bird’s-foot delta
The land that drains into one is its drainage basin, or watershed; divides like the Continental Divide separate basins
Floods spread fertile mud across flat floodplains and pile up natural levees along the banks
Where one meets the sea, fresh and salt water mix in a brackish estuary
Young, steep ones carve V-shaped valleys, unlike the U-shaped valleys carved by glaciers
Discharge is the volume of water flowing past a point each second; the Amazon’s is by far the greatest
They carry sediment as dissolved load, suspended load, and bed load, which rolls and bounces along the bottom
Braided kinds split into many shallow channels around bars of sand and gravel, often below glaciers
The word for their loops comes from the Maeander [“mee-AN-der”] in western Turkey, now called the Büyük Menderes
Their scientific study is potamology, from a Greek word that also forms part of the name “hippopotamus”
Mesopotamia’s name means the land “between” two of them, the Tigris and the Euphrates
The Hjulström [“YOOL-strum”] curve shows how fast water must flow to erode, carry, or drop grains of each size; sticky clay needs faster water than sand
In Arthur Strahler’s ordering, which built on Robert Horton’s work, two “first-order” ones (with nothing flowing in) join to make a “second-order” one
The thalweg [“TAHL-veg”], the line along the deepest channel (German for “valley way”), often marks borders; the Rio Grande’s shift caused the Chamizal dispute
John Wesley Powell, who led the first known boat trip through the Grand Canyon in 1869, named base level, the lowest point one can erode to
In capture or “piracy,” one erodes headward into the land beyond its source and steals a neighbor’s water
Yazoo-type tributaries, named for one in Mississippi, run alongside the main channel because natural levees block them
Australians call a cut-off loop a billabong, a word sung in “Waltzing Matilda”
Incised meanders like Arizona’s Horseshoe Bend (the Colorado) and Utah’s Goosenecks (the San Juan) were cut as the land rose
Land along their banks is the riparian zone (Latin for “bank”); their landforms are fluvial, and the sediment they leave is alluvium
Niagara Falls is a knickpoint, a sudden step in the slope, and has worn miles back toward Lake Erie
A hydrograph plots flow over time; lag time is the delay between peak rain and peak flow, and paving land shortens it

trap.title: Not one famous river
trap.body: Tossups on rivers in general love to name famous examples, like the Nile, the Amazon, the Mississippi, and the Colorado, so players blurt out one name. The question wants the whole category, so naming one river is wrong. Players also answer with a river’s parts or landforms, like deltas, meanders, oxbow lakes, or tributaries, which are separate answer lines.
trap.fix: Listen for “these bodies of water” or “these features.” If the tossup says “this river” and gives clues about one place, it wants a specific river, like the Mississippi River topic. Saying “streams” is fine, but lakes, deltas, and estuaries are different answers.
trap.line: Real answer line: Rivers (accept streams; do not accept “lakes,” “deltas,” or the name of a specific river)

topics.name: Asthenosphere
topics.kicker: Soft, slowly flowing layer of the upper mantle · Earth’s plates ride on it
topics.briefing: Earth’s rigid plates don’t sit on rock that stays put: they glide over the asthenosphere, a hot layer of the upper mantle that is solid but soft enough to flow very slowly, a little like Silly Putty. Its name comes from a Greek word meaning “weak.” Seismic waves slow down as they pass through it, and its slow flow lets land rise back up after the weight of ice-age glaciers melts away.
topics.answerHtml: Asthenosphere (prompt on upper mantle, mantle, or low-velocity zone; do not accept “lithosphere” or “mesosphere”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Geologist Joseph Barrell named this layer in 1914 in a series of papers on the strength of Earth’s crust, arguing that a strong outer shell must rest on something much weaker. Rock from this layer partly melts as it rises beneath mid-ocean ridges.
tossups.r: Its name comes from a Greek word meaning “weak.” For 10 points, name this soft, slowly flowing layer of the upper mantle that lies just beneath the lithosphere.

tossups.p: Clarence Dutton coined the word isostasy for the balance in which Earth’s rigid outer shell rests on this layer, like a block of wood floating in water. The heavy volcanoes of Hawaii press the seafloor down into this layer, so the islands slowly sink.
tossups.r: Earth’s tectonic plates glide over this layer. For 10 points, name this soft, flowing region of the upper mantle.

tossups.p: Where seafloor sinks at subduction zones, water squeezed out of the sinking slab rises into the hot rock of this layer just above it and lowers that rock’s melting point. The magma made there feeds chains of volcanoes like the Cascades and the volcanoes of Japan.
tossups.r: Seismic waves slow down in this layer’s low-velocity zone. For 10 points, name this weak, plastic layer of the upper mantle beneath the lithosphere.

tossups.p: Beneath mid-ocean ridges, hot rock from this layer rises and partly melts as the pressure on it drops, producing the magma that hardens into new seafloor. This layer comes closest to Earth’s surface under those ridges.
tossups.r: Slow convection currents in this layer help carry the plates along. For 10 points, name this soft, flowing layer of the upper mantle.

tossups.p: This layer’s upper boundary is set mainly by temperature rather than by any change in rock type: above it, cooler rock is stiff and strong, while below it, hotter rock of the same kind turns soft enough to flow.
tossups.r: That stiff rock above, together with the crust, forms the lithosphere. For 10 points, name this layer of the upper mantle on which tectonic plates move.

tossups.p: Unlike the crust and the mantle, which are defined by what they are made of, this layer is defined by how its rock behaves, making it a “mechanical” layer of Earth along with the lithosphere above it.
tossups.r: Some textbooks call the stiffer rock beneath it the mesosphere. For 10 points, name this soft, plastic layer of the upper mantle.

tossups.p: Like the rest of the upper mantle, this layer is made mostly of peridotite [“puh-RID-uh-tite”], a dense, green, olivine-rich rock. The same rock makes up the stiffer bottom of the lithosphere above it, but there it is cooler and stronger.
tossups.r: A tiny fraction of this layer’s rock may be melted. For 10 points, name this weak layer of the upper mantle that tectonic plates ride on.

tossups.p: As ocean floor moves away from a ridge and cools, rock from the top of this layer stiffens and joins the lithosphere, so the oldest seafloor has the thickest lithosphere. That cooling also makes old seafloor sit deeper than young seafloor.
tossups.r: Its name comes from a Greek word for “weak.” For 10 points, name this soft, slowly flowing layer of the upper mantle.

tossups.p: Ordinary earthquakes rarely start in this layer, because its hot rock bends and flows instead of snapping. The deep earthquakes that do strike at its depths happen inside cold slabs of ocean floor sinking down through it.
tossups.r: Rock in this layer is often compared to Silly Putty or warm tar. For 10 points, name this plastic layer of the upper mantle beneath the lithosphere.

tossups.p: Land around the Gulf of Bothnia, between Sweden and Finland, is still rising almost a centimeter a year, because rock in this layer is slowly flowing back after the weight of an ice-age ice sheet melted away.
tossups.r: Land around Canada’s Hudson Bay is rising for the same reason. For 10 points, name this soft, flowing layer of the upper mantle.

tossups.p: The ancient shorelines of Utah’s Lake Bonneville bulge upward near the middle of the old lake, because the land rose as rock in this layer crept back after the water drained. Grove Karl Gilbert studied those bent shorelines.
tossups.r: The rigid lithosphere floats on this layer in a balance called isostasy. For 10 points, name this layer of the upper mantle.

tossups.p: The enormous weight of Hawaii’s volcanoes bends the seafloor down into this layer, so the islands slowly sink and a moat-like trough surrounds them. That bending is possible because rock in this layer slowly gives way beneath them.
tossups.r: Earth’s tectonic plates glide over this layer. For 10 points, name this soft region of the upper mantle beneath the lithosphere.

tossups.p: Seismic S-waves slow down sharply in the upper part of this layer, called the low-velocity zone, a sign that its rock is hot, soft, and possibly very slightly melted. Its top lies roughly 100 kilometers down, and deeper beneath old continents.
tossups.r: Tectonic plates slide over it. For 10 points, name this layer whose name comes from the Greek word for “weak.”

tossups.p: Some textbooks divide Earth by stiffness into the lithosphere, this layer, and a stronger zone below it called the mesosphere, which shares its name with a layer of the atmosphere. Hot plumes of rock push up through this layer beneath hotspots like Iceland.
tossups.r: Slow convection currents in this layer help move the plates above. For 10 points, name this soft, plastic layer of the upper mantle.

tossups.p: Rock in this layer is solid, but it is so hot that over thousands of years it flows like Silly Putty or warm tar, bending instead of breaking. Geologists call rock that behaves this way plastic or ductile.
tossups.r: Earth’s rigid lithosphere rides on top of it. For 10 points, name this soft layer of the upper mantle, whose name comes from the Greek for “weak.”

clues.t: A hot, soft layer of the upper mantle that is solid but flows very slowly
Lies just beneath the rigid lithosphere, which is the crust plus the stiff top of the mantle
Earth’s tectonic plates glide over it
Its name comes from a Greek word meaning “weak” or “without strength”
Its rock is plastic, or ductile: it bends and flows instead of breaking, and is often compared to Silly Putty or warm tar
Slow convection currents in it help carry the plates along
Seismic waves, especially S-waves, slow down in its upper part, the low-velocity zone
Nearly all of its rock is solid, but a tiny fraction may be melted, which helps make it weak
Some textbooks call the stiffer rock below it the mesosphere, the same name as a layer of the atmosphere
The lithosphere floats on it in a balance called isostasy, like a block of wood floating in water
Its slow flow lets land rise back up after ice-age ice sheets melt, as around Canada’s Hudson Bay
Its top lies roughly 100 kilometers down: shallower under mid-ocean ridges and deeper under old continents
Hot plumes of rock rising through the mantle push up through it beneath hotspots like Iceland and Hawaii
Named in 1914 by geologist Joseph Barrell, in papers on the strength of Earth’s crust
Clarence Dutton coined the word “isostasy” for the floating balance of the rigid shell above it
At subduction zones, water from a sinking slab lowers the melting point of its hot rock, making magma for volcanoes like the Cascades
Beneath mid-ocean ridges, its rock rises and partly melts as the pressure drops, making the magma for new seafloor
Its top boundary is set by temperature, not rock type: the same rock is stiff when cooler above and soft when hotter below
A “mechanical” layer, defined by how its rock behaves, unlike the crust and mantle, which are defined by what they are made of
Made mostly of peridotite [“puh-RID-uh-tite”], a dense, green, olivine-rich rock
As seafloor ages and cools, rock from its top stiffens and joins the lithosphere, so the oldest seafloor has the thickest lithosphere
Ordinary earthquakes rarely start in it because its rock bends instead of snapping; deep quakes strike only inside cold sinking slabs
Land around the Gulf of Bothnia, between Sweden and Finland, is still rising almost a centimeter a year as rock in it flows back
Utah’s ancient Lake Bonneville shorelines, studied by G. K. Gilbert, bulge upward where the land rose after the lake drained
Hawaii’s heavy volcanoes bend the seafloor down into it, so the islands slowly sink inside a moat-like trough

trap.title: Asthenosphere or lithosphere?
trap.body: Both names end in “-sphere,” and the two layers sit right on top of each other. The lithosphere is the rigid outer shell (the crust plus the stiff top of the mantle) that is broken into tectonic plates, while the asthenosphere is the soft, slowly flowing layer just beneath it that the plates ride on. Players also answer “mantle,” which is too broad, because the asthenosphere is only one part of the upper mantle.
trap.fix: Rigid, brittle, broken into plates, or includes the crust means lithosphere. Soft, plastic, flowing, Greek for “weak,” the low-velocity zone, or the layer the plates glide on means asthenosphere. “Upper mantle” or “mantle” earns only a prompt, and the mesosphere is the stiffer zone below it (or a layer of the atmosphere).
trap.line: Real answer line: Asthenosphere (prompt on upper mantle or mantle; do not accept “lithosphere” or “mesosphere”)

topics.name: Magma
topics.kicker: Molten rock beneath Earth’s surface · Called lava once it erupts
topics.briefing: Magma is melted rock: a hot, thick mixture of liquid, crystals, and dissolved gases that forms deep underground and collects in chambers beneath volcanoes. Once it pours or blasts out onto the surface, it is called lava. Runny, low-silica magma like Hawaii’s oozes out in glowing streams, but thick, silica-rich magma traps its gases until they explode, the way a shaken soda bursts when you open it.
topics.answerHtml: Magma (accept lava; prompt on molten rock or melted rock; do not accept “magma chamber,” “volcano,” or “igneous rock”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: This substance’s name comes from a Greek word for a thick, kneaded paste. Wind can stretch flying droplets of it into golden threads of volcanic glass called Pele’s hair, named for the Hawaiian volcano goddess.
tossups.r: It is a hot mixture of liquid rock, crystals, and dissolved gases. For 10 points, name this molten rock found beneath Earth’s surface.

tossups.p: In 2009, engineers drilling for geothermal energy at Krafla in Iceland accidentally struck a pocket of this substance about two kilometers down. That pocket turned out to be rich in silica, the ingredient that makes this substance thick and sticky.
tossups.r: Thick, gas-rich kinds of this substance erupt explosively, like a shaken soda. For 10 points, name this molten rock that erupts from volcanoes.

tossups.p: Tanzania’s Ol Doinyo Lengai, whose name means “Mountain of God” in the Maasai language, erupts the coolest known kind of this substance, a carbonate-rich type that flows out black, turns white within days, and is far runnier than ordinary kinds.
tossups.r: Most of this substance is roughly 700 to 1,300 degrees Celsius, with runny basaltic kinds the hottest. For 10 points, name this molten rock that erupts from volcanoes.

tossups.p: Kimberlite, a rare kind of this substance that races up from deep in the mantle, carries diamonds to the surface through carrot-shaped pipes. It rises so fast that the diamonds have no time to turn into graphite on the way up.
tossups.r: When this substance cools underground instead of erupting, it forms plutons such as dikes and sills. For 10 points, name this molten rock found beneath Earth’s surface.

tossups.p: The young Moon was covered by an ocean of this substance hundreds of kilometers deep, and light crystals that floated to its top formed the bright lunar highlands. Early Earth was probably covered by a similar ocean after a giant impact.
tossups.r: This substance cools into igneous rocks such as basalt and granite. For 10 points, name this molten rock, which gets a different name once it erupts onto the surface.

tossups.p: Jupiter’s moon Io erupts more of this substance than any other world in the solar system, because tides raised by Jupiter keep its interior hot. A giant pit on Io called Loki Patera seems to hold an enormous lake of it.
tossups.r: On Earth, this substance collects in underground chambers beneath volcanoes. For 10 points, name this molten rock.

tossups.p: Beneath Yellowstone National Park lies a huge reservoir of this substance that is mostly a crystal-rich “mush,” with only a small fraction actually melted. Its heat powers the park’s geysers and hot springs, and the ground above it slowly rises and sinks over the years.
tossups.r: When a chamber of this substance empties in a giant eruption, the ground above can collapse into a caldera. For 10 points, name this molten rock.

tossups.p: Early-forming crystals like olivine can sink to the floor of an underground body of this substance and pile up in layers, leaving the remaining liquid richer in silica. Norman Bowen’s reaction series describes the order in which those minerals crystallize.
tossups.r: The more silica this substance holds, the thicker and stickier it is. For 10 points, name this molten rock found beneath Earth’s surface.

tossups.p: At subduction zones, water released from the sinking seafloor lowers the melting point of the hot mantle rock above it, a process called flux melting that produces this substance. That is why chains of volcanoes line deep-ocean trenches.
tossups.r: Its dissolved gases, mostly water vapor and carbon dioxide, bubble out as it rises. For 10 points, name this molten rock found beneath Earth’s surface.

tossups.p: Beneath mid-ocean ridges and hotspots, hot mantle rock rising toward the surface melts into this substance as the pressure on it drops, a process called decompression melting. Iceland sits on both a mid-ocean ridge and a hotspot.
tossups.r: Erupting underwater, this substance cools quickly into rounded pillows. For 10 points, name this molten rock that erupts from volcanoes.

tossups.p: Rising bodies of this substance can make room for themselves by stoping, in which blocks of the rock above break off and sink into them, and by assimilation, in which they melt and absorb the surrounding rock.
tossups.r: When this substance cools underground, it forms intrusive bodies called plutons. For 10 points, name this molten rock that is the source of all igneous rocks.

tossups.p: Ethiopia’s Erta Ale and Nyiragongo [“neer-ah-GONG-goh”], in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, are famous for long-lasting lakes of this substance glowing inside their craters. A thin crust keeps forming on top of those lakes and cracking apart as the hot liquid below churns.
tossups.r: Hawaiian words name its smooth, ropy pahoehoe [“pa-HOH-ay-HOH-ay”] flows and rough, jagged a‘a [“AH-ah”] flows. For 10 points, name this molten rock that erupts from volcanoes.

tossups.p: Droplets of this substance that harden in midair into tiny teardrop-shaped beads of glass are called Pele’s tears, after the Hawaiian volcano goddess. Thin golden threads of glass spun from it by the wind are called Pele’s hair.
tossups.r: Runny, low-silica kinds of this substance erupt gently in Hawaii. For 10 points, name this molten rock that erupts from volcanoes.

tossups.p: In the spring of 1980, a body of this substance pushing up inside Mount St. Helens made the volcano’s north side bulge outward by more than a meter a day. That bulge collapsed in a giant landslide that set off the May 18 eruption.
tossups.r: Thick, gas-rich kinds of this substance trap bubbles until they explode. For 10 points, name this molten rock that collects in chambers beneath volcanoes.

tossups.p: This substance’s viscosity, or thickness, depends mostly on how much silica it contains: silica-rich kinds are sticky and trap gas, while silica-poor kinds are runny and let gas escape. That difference decides whether a volcano explodes or oozes.
tossups.r: This substance cools into igneous rocks like granite and basalt. For 10 points, name this molten rock found beneath Earth’s surface.

Tanzania’s Ol Doinyo Lengai (“Mountain of God”) erupts the coolest known kind, a carbonate-rich type that comes out black and turns white
Kimberlite, a kind that races up from deep in the mantle, carries diamonds up through carrot-shaped pipes

Early crystals like olivine sink out of it and pile up in layers, leaving the leftover liquid richer in silica: fractional crystallization

It makes room by stoping (blocks of roof rock break off and sink into it) and by assimilation (melting and absorbing nearby rock)

trap.title: Magma or lava?
trap.body: They are the same molten rock in two places: magma is underground, and lava is what it is called once it erupts onto the surface. This site accepts both, but some real answer lines want only one, so a question about magma chambers, plutons, or melting deep underground may reject or only prompt on lava, and a question about pahoehoe flows may want lava. The volcano itself, the magma chamber, and the igneous rock that it cools into are all different answers.
trap.fix: Underground clues (chambers, plutons, flux or decompression melting, Bowen’s reaction series) mean say “magma.” Surface clues (flows, pahoehoe and a‘a, Pele’s hair, lakes in craters) mean say “lava.” Saying only “molten rock” earns a prompt.
trap.line: Real answer line: Magma (accept lava; prompt on molten rock; do not accept “magma chamber,” “volcano,” or “igneous rock”)
